title: In-Context Learning Can Help Vision Language Models Overcome Training Prior
claim: Demonstrations let models override a learned prior and follow visual evidence, with gains on conflicting inputs, shown by behavior and mechanism.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: example, scaling plot, mechanism bars; red vs green coding
description: A three-panel figure with rounded borders, labeled A, B and C. Panel A, 'Training Prior', shows a photo of a peacock and the question 'How many legs does this animal have?'. A red box for zero-shot shows the answer '2' with a crossed arrow to a 'Training Prior' tag. A green box for ICL shows three demo animal photos labeled 5, 3 and 4, with answer '3' and a check mark leading to a 'Visual Grounded' tag. Panel B, 'Scaling of Visual ICL', is a line plot of accuracy against ICL shots from zero-shot to 32. The blue real-image line stays near 90–93%. The red dashed counterfactual line climbs from about 52% to 79%, with a green bracket labeled +27.2%. Panel C, 'Mechanistic Shift', shows the peacock with a logit-lens magnifier. Below it, a bar chart shows attention falling for 'Peacock' (red, -2.91) and rising for 'Leg' (green, +1.21).
caption: Visual ICL overcomes \prior dominance. (A) A VLM answers "2" for a three-legged peacock under zero-shot prompting; label-balanced demonstrations shift the answer to the visually grounded "3." (B) Scaling ICL shots yields a $+27.2$ pp accuracy gain on counterfactual images while real images remain near ceiling. (C) Mechanistically, demonstrations redirect attention from the prior cue ("peacock") to the grounding cue ("leg").
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) learn strong statistical regularities during training, which can make them fail to properly respond to visual evidence when input images violate those regularities. It is challenging to disambiguate these prior-induced errors from errors caused by the model missing the underlying visual capabilities. In this work, we use controlled visual in-context learning to encourage the model to focus on the visual evidence, and demonstrate that this alone is frequently sufficient to correct the errors -- suggesting that the models in fact do possess the relevant visual capabilities. Specifically, we show that across five vision-centric tasks, demonstrations yield large gains on prior-conflicting counterfactual examples ($+27.2\%$ for Qwen3-VL 235B and $+15.1\%$ for Qwen3-VL 32B) while leaving accuracy on prior-aligned examples nearly unchanged. These findings generalize across five VLM families with gains from $+9.7\%$ to $+30.3\%$. We analyze visual representations and find that demonstrations indeed redirect attention toward grounding cues while reducing reliance on cues that support the learned prior. Finally, we find that in-context learning is limited when the underlying visual capability is weak or absent. Together, these results show that current VLMs possess visual grounding capabilities that standard evaluations may overlook, underscoring the need for controlled evaluation design in diagnosing and improving model capability.
